The Whiskey Ring. A nationwide conspiracy that revealed how deep corruption could run through the executive branch itself during the Grant administration.

Between 1870 and 1874, whiskey distillers and federal tax collectors conspired in multiple states. St. Louis. Chicago. Philadelphia. Galena. They falsified tax records to defraud the federal government of whiskey excise taxes. It was organized, systematic theft.

The ring falsified internal revenue documents. This allowed distillers to sell whiskey that had never been taxed. Federal officers pocketed bribes from the producers. The government lost between two and three million dollars every year to this scheme.

In 1874, Secretary of the Treasury Benjamin Bristow launched an investigation. Bristow wasn't implicated in the corruption himself. He was trying to clean it up. He launched raids. He made arrests of dozens of conspirators, including federal agents and prominent distillers themselves.

Over two hundred and thirty indictments were issued. More than one hundred and ten convictions resulted. The public was shocked. Evidence of systemic corruption within the executive branch itself was laid bare.

But then things got murky. President Grant's private secretary, Orville Babcock, was implicated in the conspiracy. The question became: how high did this go? Did it reach the president himself?

Grant defended Babcock. He stood by his secretary. Babcock was tried but acquitted in 1876, partly due to Grant's intervention and support. The administration's apparent complicity undermined Bristow's efforts and tarnished Grant's entire presidency. The scandal fueled calls for civil service reform. It exposed how vulnerable the federal revenue system was to organized corruption. The Treasury Secretary Benjamin Bristow was the one who exposed the conspiracy courageously, even as his president stood in his way. Ulysses S. Grant was the president whose administration was implicated in covering up the scheme. Orville Babcock was Grant's secretary whose acquittal despite apparent guilt damaged public trust in justice itself. And the scandal became emblematic of Reconstruction era corruption, exposing how thoroughly the post-Civil War government had been infiltrated by graft and bribery.
